segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For freedom Christ set us free. Stand firm, then, and do not let yourselves be held again by a yoke of slavery.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Look: I, Paul, tell you that if you let yourselves be circumcised, Christ will be of no benefit to you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And I testify again to every man who lets himself be circumcised that he is obligated to keep the whole law.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: You have been severed from Christ, you who are trying to be justified by law; you have fallen away from grace.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For we, by the Spirit, on the basis of faith, eagerly await the hope of righteousness.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts for anything; what counts is faith working through love.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: You were running well. Who cut in on you to keep you from being persuaded by the truth?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: This persuasion does not come from the one who calls you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: A little leaven leavens the whole batch of dough.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I am persuaded about you in the Lord that you will take no other view. But the one who is troubling you will bear the judgment, whoever he may be.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But as for me, brothers and sisters, if I am still preaching circumcision, why am I still being persecuted? In that case the stumbling block of the cross has been done away with.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I wish those who are unsettling you would go so far as to castrate themselves!

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For you were called to freedom, brothers and sisters. Only do not let that freedom become an opening for the flesh, but through love be slaves to one another.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the whole law is fulfilled in a single saying:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But if you bite and devour one another, watch out that you are not consumed by one another.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But I say: walk by the Spirit, and you will never carry out the desire of the flesh.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the flesh sets its desire against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh; these are opposed to each other, so that you do not do whatever you want.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But if you are led by the Spirit, you are not under law.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now the works of the flesh are obvious: sexual immorality, impurity, debauchery,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: idolatry, sorcery, hostilities, strife, jealousy, outbursts of rage, selfish rivalries, dissensions, factions,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: envy, drunkenness, carousing, and things like these. About these I tell you in advance, just as I told you before, that those who practice such things will not inherit the kingdom of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: gentleness, self-control. Against such things there is no law.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: If we live by the Spirit, let us also keep in step with the Spirit.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Let us not become conceited, provoking one another, envying one another.

notes.traditional: “Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free” (KJV); “For freedom Christ has set us free” in most modern versions
notes.note: The Greek phrase can mean “for freedom” (the purpose of the liberation) or “by freedom” (its means); the first is the majority view and is followed here. Later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, attach the phrase to the command instead: “Stand firm in the freedom with which Christ set us free.”

notes.traditional: “Christ is become of no effect unto you” (KJV); “severed” or “alienated” in modern versions
notes.note: The verb means to put something out of operation; in the passive with “from” it means to be discharged or cut off from something. The same verb returns in verse 11, where the stumbling block of the cross would be “done away with”. English has no single word that fits both uses.

Greek has one word-family where English has two: “justified” here and “righteousness” in verse 5 share a root, as “just” and “justice” do. The present tense describes an attempt under way, not an accomplished fact, hence “trying to be”.

The phrase can mean the righteousness that is hoped for, that is, God’s final verdict, or the hope that belongs to those already counted righteous. Most interpreters prefer the first. The rendering is left as open as the Greek.

The verb can mean “obey”, and most translations render it so here. “Persuaded” is used because Paul plays on the same root three times in four verses: being persuaded by the truth (verse 7), “this persuasion” (verse 8) and “I am persuaded” (verse 10). “Obey” hides the link.

notes.traditional: “I would they were even cut off” (KJV); “castrate” or “emasculate” in most modern versions
notes.note: The verb means “cut off”, and it echoes “cut in on” in verse 7. Paul’s bitter joke is that those so eager to cut the foreskin should carry the knife further. Older versions softened this to exclusion from the community, but the reference to castration is the standard scholarly view.

The verb is the ordinary one for a slave’s service and belongs to the same word-family as “slavery” in verse 1. The paradox is deliberate: those freed from the yoke of slavery are to be slaves to each other through love. Most translations soften it to “serve”, though some have “become slaves”.

In this chapter “flesh” is not the body as such but human nature left to itself, weak and self-centered, as opposed to life directed by God’s Spirit. The list in verses 19–21 includes strife and envy, which are not bodily sins. Some translations paraphrase as “sinful nature”; the traditional word is kept, partly because the letter also uses it of the literal flesh cut in circumcision.

notes.phrase: so that you do not do whatever you want
notes.traditional: so that ye cannot do the things that ye would
notes.note: The clause may express the result of the conflict or its purpose. “Whatever you want” may be the good a person wishes to do, which the flesh blocks; the evil the flesh craves, which the Spirit blocks; or both. Interpreters are divided, and the rendering does not decide between them.

Many later manuscripts add “murders” after “envy”; the two Greek words look and sound alike. The King James Version includes it. Important early manuscripts lack it, and the SBLGNT text translated here omits it.

This is the same Greek word translated “faith” in verses 5 and 6. In a list of qualities shown toward other people, it most likely means reliability or trustworthiness, and most modern translations agree. Some interpreters take it as trust in God.
“Meekness” now suggests weakness or timidity, which the Greek word does not. It describes someone who is not harsh or self-assertive. “Gentleness” is the usual rendering in modern translations.

candidates.reason: Paul’s ethical use is rendered “flesh”, “sinful nature” or “human nature” across versions, and the choice must be uniform across Romans, Galatians and elsewhere.
The plural address to mixed congregations recurs in every letter and needs one decision between “brothers” and “brothers and sisters”.
The figurative sense of conduct is rendered “walk” or “live” by different translators, and the Semitic idiom should be handled the same way throughout.
Translators vary between “serve” and “be a slave to”, and the choice should match whatever is decided for δοῦλος.
It recurs in vice lists and in the Gospels and Acts, with “fornication”, “sexual immorality” and “prostitution” all in use; readers should see one term.
